title: Grade tiers with exact-match lookup
summary: Turn a customer grade label into a discount rate with XLOOKUP, and see why exact match needs labels rather than number bands.

blocks.text: A wholesale team gives trade customers a discount based on their grade: A, B, C or D. The discount table lists each grade once with its rate. Each order line carries the customer's grade, and you need the discount in K and the net order value.

This works well with XLOOKUP because a grade is a label that appears exactly in the table. Customers are often graded from a score, such as 0 to 100. A score cannot be looked up directly. You will see why, and what to do about it.

items: Objective: use a label column (grades A to D) as the key of an exact-match XLOOKUP, and explain why number bands do not work for exact match.
You pass the mission at 75% or more in the Assessment.

blocks.caption: Discount table in H1:I5 (rates are decimals: 0.1 means 10%)

blocks.text: Look for the grade in B2 in the grade column and return its rate. The fourth argument 0 means: if the grade is not in the table, use a rate of 0, so the discount calculation still works. Case does not matter, so b finds B.
For a grade B order of 600K, the rate is 0.07, the discount is 600 x 0.07 = 42K and the net order is 600 - 42 = 558K.
Why labels? XLOOKUP in this course matches exactly. Suppose a score table lists only the starting score of each band.

blocks.caption: Score bands (a table that does NOT work with exact match)

blocks.text: A score of 73 is not in the list: it falls inside the band that starts at 70. An exact-match XLOOKUP of 73 gives #N/A. Only a score of exactly 0, 50, 70 or 85 would be found.

The fix is a two-step approach. First turn the score in S2 into a grade label with a nested IF, as in the earlier IF missions. Then look the grade label up in the discount table with an exact-match XLOOKUP.

items: Exact match needs the key to appear in the table exactly. Use a label column such as the grade, not number bands.
Give the fourth argument a number such as 0 when the result is used in arithmetic. A text message would cause #VALUE! in the next formula.
Keep the grade labels spelled the same in the order sheet and in the table.

blocks.text: Use the discount table and the score bands from Training. Give percentages as plain numbers, for example 4 for 4%.

items: Exact-match XLOOKUP needs the key to appear exactly in the table.
Use a label column such as A, B, C, D as the key, not number bands.
For scores, turn the score into a label with IF first, then look up the label.
Give the fourth argument a number like 0 when the result feeds arithmetic.

blocks.text: Labels make lookups exact and reliable, so build a label first and look it up second.

items.prompt: What discount percentage does =XLOOKUP("C",$H$2:$H$5,$I$2:$I$5,0) give? Answer as a percentage, for example 4 for 4%.
